analysis.one_liner: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set a fire safety standard for cigarettes.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a markup or a floor vote, despite having a Democratic sponsor and a Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write a rule requiring cigarettes to be less likely to start fires, and to ban the manufacture or import of cigarettes that don't meet the standard. It also would have barred manufacturers from rushing out extra noncompliant cigarettes before the rule took effect, and stopped cigarette makers from using compliance with the new standard as a defense in fire-damage lawsuits. Cigarette-ignited fires were the leading cause of fire deaths in the United States, killing more than 1,000 people a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — especially smokers' families, children, renters, and homeowners — who lose lives, health, homes, and property to fires started by cigarettes. The bill's findings cite 1,083 deaths, 2,809 civilian injuries, and $420 million in property damage in 1996 alone, and a CPSC estimate of $6 billion a year in losses from the absence of a standard [S3]. State and local fire services also benefit from fewer fires.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families and victims of cigarette fires

how_it_helps.text: Cigarette-ignited fires are the leading cause of fire deaths in the United States; in 1996 they caused 1,083 deaths, 2,809 civilian injuries, and $420 million in property damage, and more than 100 children are killed each year in cigarette-related fires [S3].
The CPSC estimated the annual cost of the loss of human life and property from the absence of a cigarette fire safety standard at $6 billion [S3].

The technical work for a standard had already been completed under the Cigarette Safety Act of 1984 and the Fire Safe Cigarette Act of 1990, and a prior CPSC report found that low-ignition-propensity cigarettes were already on the market — meaning the change was technically feasible when the bill was introduced [S3].

The bill lets states keep or adopt stricter cigarette fire safety standards than the federal rule, and bars cigarette makers from arguing in fire-damage lawsuits that compliance with the federal standard shields them from liability [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cigarette manufacturers, who would have to redesign or restrict their products to meet a fire safety standard within 30 months of enactment, and importers of noncompliant cigarettes. Any compliance costs could be passed along to smokers in cigarette prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Complying with a fire safety standard would impose real manufacturing costs on cigarette companies, and some or all of those costs would likely show up in cigarette prices paid by smokers [S3].

The bill waives several layers of normal regulatory process — it directs the rule to be written outside the ordinary Consumer Product Safety Act procedures and exempts the standard from Small Business Act review — trading regulatory speed for less process [S3].
A standard makes cigarettes safer but does nothing to reduce smoking itself, and critics could argue it may make a lethal product seem less risky.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are measured in lives — over a thousand fire deaths a year, more than a hundred of them children — against compliance costs to an industry selling a product that was the leading cause of U.S. fire deaths, using technology that already existed on the market. The main honest cost is to smokers' pocketbooks if compliance costs are passed through.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Fire Safe Cigarette Act of 1999 on March 25, 1999 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cigarette manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided a federal mandate to make fire-safe cigarettes and the enforcement and litigation exposure that came with it, while the estimated 1,083 people a year dying in cigarette-ignited fires gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: 1 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (chaired by Sen. John McCain)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out during the Congress

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: The industry had long opposed mandatory fire-safe cigarette standards; the bill would have forced compliance on all U.S. cigarette production and imports

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat introduced it and one Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would have required every cigarette sold or imported in the U.S. to meet a fire safety standard within 30 months, banned stockpiling of noncompliant cigarettes, and barred the industry from using compliance as a liability defense in fire lawsuits. Low-ignition-propensity cigarettes already existed on the market, so the mandate forced a change the industry had not made voluntarily.

Fewer cigarette-ignited fires — which caused $420 million in property damage in 1996 — would mean fewer fire claims paid by insurers, a benefit that runs alongside the public's interest in fewer fire deaths.
Fire departments and emergency services respond to more than a thousand cigarette-fire deaths and thousands of injuries a year; a fire safety standard would reduce that burden.
